prompt: The lapse model's accuracy is 86.0%. Why is that not evidence of a good model?

choices.text: Saying nobody lapses already scores 83.1%
choices.why: Right. Most members stay, so accuracy mostly measures that.

choices.text: Accuracy cannot be computed for logistic regression
choices.why: It can, and it was: 86.0%.

choices.text: 86% is below the 90% a production model is expected to reach
choices.why: There is no such bar; the problem is what the number compares with.

choices.text: The test month had unfinished labels
choices.why: 30 November's window closed on 28 February.

prompt: What accuracy does the model that says nobody lapses reach on 30 November, in percent?
A fraud model never flags anything and scores 99.9% accuracy. What does that tell you about fraud in the data?

choices.text: That the model catches 99.9% of the fraud
choices.why: It catches none: it never flags anything.

choices.text: That it is about one payment in a thousand
choices.why: Right. The score is the share of the common outcome.

choices.text: That fraud is too rare to model at all
choices.why: Rare outcomes are modelled every day; they need other scores.

choices.text: That the payments data has leaked the label
choices.why: No leak is needed to score that; ignoring the rare class does it.

prompt: Why does lesson 4 put the lapse model's definition in model.py?

choices.text: Because scikit-learn requires models to live in their own file
choices.why: It requires nothing of the kind.

choices.text: To make the model train faster
choices.why: Where it is defined changes nothing about speed.

choices.text: So the model has one definition in the project
choices.why: Right. Every program that needs it imports it, and lesson 5 depends on that.

choices.text: To hide the threshold from the other programs
choices.why: There is no threshold in it; the probabilities come out whole.

prompt: Match each cell of the confusion matrix to its count at 0.5.
What does a false alarm cost Ponto Final?

choices.text: A member who leaves without anybody trying
choices.why: That is a miss, the other kind of error.

choices.text: Nothing, because the member stays
choices.why: The voucher was still paid for.

choices.text: A retraining of the model
choices.why: One wrong prediction retrains nothing.

choices.text: A voucher sent to somebody who was coming back anyway
choices.why: Right. The two errors cost different amounts, which is why they are counted apart.

prompt: At the 0.5 threshold, what is the model's recall?
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 does what to precision and recall?

choices.text: Recall rises and precision falls
Both rise, because more members are flagged
choices.why: More flags catch more lapses and also more members who were staying.

choices.text: Precision rises and recall falls
choices.why: That is raising the threshold.

choices.text: Neither moves; they are properties of the model
choices.why: A model has a precision at every threshold.

prompt: Why does F1 not help choose a threshold?

choices.text: It is only defined at 0.5
choices.why: It can be computed at any threshold.

choices.text: It weighs precision and recall equally, hiding the trade
choices.why: Right. A voucher and a lost member are never the same amount of money.

choices.text: It ignores the false alarms entirely
choices.why: False alarms enter through precision.

choices.text: It is the same number as accuracy
choices.why: It is built from precision and recall, not from the four cells equally.

prompt: At R$ 10.00 a voucher and R$ 60.00 a member kept, which threshold gave the most net value?

choices.text: 0.5, scikit-learn's default
choices.why: It was worth R$ 7,720.00, well below the best.

choices.text: 0.1, because it catches the most lapses
choices.why: It catches more and pays for 1,688 vouchers.
Right. R$ 11,900.00, with 742 vouchers.

choices.text: 0.6, because its precision is highest
choices.why: High precision on 180 vouchers leaves most lapses uncaught.

prompt: By the rule of thumb, a voucher pays for itself above what probability, with a R$ 10 voucher and a R$ 60 member? Give two decimals.
Marketing says: we can send exactly 300 vouchers this month. What changes?

choices.text: The threshold must be recomputed from the new costs
choices.why: There are no new costs, only a limit.

choices.text: The model must be retrained on 300 members
choices.why: The budget changes how the output is used, not the model.

choices.text: Accuracy becomes the right score again
choices.why: Nothing about a budget rescues accuracy.

choices.text: There is no threshold to choose: sort and take the top 300
choices.why: Right. The score is then how many of those 300 lapse.

prompt: What does a model that flags members at random score on average precision here?

choices.text: 0.169, the share who lapse
choices.why: Right. Random flags hit lapsers at the rate they occur.

choices.text: 0.5, like a coin on AUC
choices.why: That is AUC's coin; average precision's is the base rate.

choices.text: Zero, since it learned nothing
choices.why: Random flags still hit some lapsing members.

choices.text: 0.522, the same as the model
choices.why: 0.522 is the model's lift over 0.169.

prompt: Of the top 300 members by probability, how many lapsed?
Match each question to the score that answers it.

pairs.left: Does the model order members well, in general?

prompt: Why is ROC AUC blind to how rare the positive class is?

choices.text: It uses a threshold of 0.5
choices.why: It uses every threshold at once.

choices.text: It only compares pairs of one lapsed and one staying member
choices.why: Right. How many of each there are never enters the number.

choices.text: It is computed on the training rows
choices.why: ranking.py computes it on the test month.

choices.text: It ignores the members who stayed
choices.why: Every pair has one member who stayed.

prompt: What does it mean for the lapse model to be calibrated?

choices.text: It ranks every lapsed member above every staying one
choices.why: That is a perfect AUC, a different property.

choices.text: It was retrained this month
choices.why: Freshness and calibration are different things.

choices.text: Its 0.3 really means a 30% chance
choices.why: Right. Then its probabilities can be multiplied by costs.

choices.text: Its threshold was set at the cost ratio
choices.why: That rule relies on calibration; it does not create it.

prompt: Over all members on 30 November, what average probability of lapsing did the model give? Three decimals.
If the share of members who lapse doubles next quarter, which score notices first, once the labels arrive?

choices.text: ROC AUC, because the order of members changes
choices.why: The order can stay roughly right while every probability is wrong.

choices.text: Precision at 100, because the top hundred move
choices.why: The top of the list can stay full of lapsers.

choices.text: Accuracy, because more members lapse
choices.why: Accuracy mixes the change with everything else.

choices.text: The calibration table
choices.why: Right. Said and happened drift apart in every band.

prompt: Why is RMSE about R$ 50 larger than MAE for the spend regression?

choices.text: A few members spent far more than predicted, and squaring weighs them heavily
choices.why: Right. R$ 1,637.20 against a prediction near R$ 300.

choices.text: RMSE is in cents and MAE in reais
choices.why: errors.py puts both in reais.

choices.text: The regression overfits its training rows
choices.why: The baseline shows the same gap, and it fits nothing.

choices.text: Because MAE ignores members who spent nothing
choices.why: Those members count, with a label of 0.

prompt: Match each score to what it is sensitive to.

pairs.right: large errors much more than small

right_distractors: the share of members who lapse

prompt: A shop runs out of a book when the forecast is too low, and that costs far more than a few extra copies. Which score fits?

choices.text: The median absolute error, because it describes the typical day
choices.why: It ignores exactly the large misses that cost most.

choices.text: RMSE
choices.why: Right. It weighs a large miss much more than a small one.

choices.text: Accuracy
choices.why: An amount has no accuracy; it is near or far.

choices.text: Average precision, because stock-outs are rare
choices.why: That scores a ranking of yes-or-no answers, not an amount.

prompt: What should be logged beside every score, according to the lesson?

choices.text: The name of the person who computed it
choices.why: Useful, but it does not make the number comparable.

choices.text: The threshold of 0.5
choices.why: Several of the scores need no threshold at all.

choices.text: Its baseline and the rows it was computed on
choices.why: Right. AUC 0.790 means nothing without the month and the 530 of 3,130.

choices.text: Only the deciding score; the others are noise
choices.why: The others are watched, because calibration breaks quietly.

prompt: In this lesson's division of work, what does the platform guarantee about scores?

choices.text: That they are always above the previous model's
choices.why: Nothing can guarantee that.

choices.text: Which score decides the release
choices.why: That is agreed with the people who use the model.

choices.text: That accuracy is never computed
choices.why: It can be computed; it just must not decide.

choices.text: Computed the same way, on rows not used for choosing, and stored
choices.why: Right. The modeller chooses which scores make sense.

prompt: Two lapse models: A has AUC 0.80 and is badly calibrated, B has AUC 0.78 and is calibrated. Marketing will set the threshold from costs. Which should ship?

choices.text: B
choices.why: Right. A cost-based threshold needs believable probabilities; A would need recalibrating first.

choices.text: A, because AUC is the deciding score for a ranking
choices.why: Here the use multiplies probabilities by costs, so they must be right.

choices.text: Neither, since both are below 0.9
choices.why: No such bar exists.

choices.text: Whichever has the higher accuracy
choices.why: Accuracy is the trap this lesson is named for.
